justice: The street space is dominated by a central shared carriageway, while no clearly protected sidewalk is visible, suggesting limited equitable allocation of space for pedestrians compared with vehicles.

A parked van occupies the right edge of the lane and residential items such as tables, planters, and miscellaneous objects spread into the left frontage, indicating uneven and informal use of public space.

The pavement appears mostly level without obvious steps across the roadway, which offers some basic physical accessibility, but there are no marked curb ramps, tactile paving, or dedicated accessible paths visible.
No dedicated bike lane, marked pedestrian zone, or crossing facility is visible, so different user groups do not appear to receive clearly differentiated and fair movement space.
safety: There is no visible sidewalk separation, bollard line, or curb protection between pedestrians and moving vehicles, increasing conflict risk in this narrow residential lane.
The right side is heavily shaded by large trees, which may reduce daytime visibility and natural surveillance along part of the street.
A parked van on the right narrows the usable roadway and can create sightline obstruction for drivers, walkers, and potential cyclists.
The residential setting has low apparent traffic speed and limited through movement, which somewhat reduces severe crash risk compared with a major arterial road.
livability: Large mature trees on the right provide greenery and contribute to a more habitable residential atmosphere.
Ground-level domestic activity, laundry on balconies, and visible household use of outdoor space suggest an inhabited and socially active neighborhood environment.
However, the street lacks clear public amenities such as benches, play elements, storefronts, or organized community space that would support richer daily street life.
Informal storage and scattered objects near the building frontage reduce the sense of order and everyday usability of the shared open space.
sustainability: The mature tree canopy on the right side provides ecological value, shade, and some microclimate regulation.
The compact residential form with multi-story apartment buildings supports relatively efficient land use.
No visible bike facilities, transit stop infrastructure, or dedicated low-carbon mobility amenities are present in the scene.
Most of the ground surface is hard paving, and no obvious permeable landscape strip, bioswale, or rainwater management feature can be identified.
aesthetics: The large trees add visual softness and natural contrast to the otherwise hard-built environment.
Building facades are repetitive and utilitarian, with extensive window grilles and enclosed balconies that create a more defensive than elegant appearance.
Visible clutter from tables, containers, hanging laundry, and miscellaneous frontage items lowers visual coherence.
The parked van in the foreground and the plain paved roadway further weaken the streetscape's overall visual quality.
comfort: The tree canopy on the right offers substantial shade, improving thermal comfort for people using that side of the street.
In contrast, the left side near the building frontage is more exposed to direct sun and has limited planted buffering.
The roadway surface appears generally flat and even, which supports basic physical comfort for walking and slow cycling.
There are no visible benches, formal resting places, or clearly designated pedestrian refuges, reducing comfort for longer stays and slower users.
The enclosed residential lane likely has lower traffic noise than a main road, supporting moderate psychological comfort despite the somewhat dim and cluttered setting.
walkability: No continuous dedicated sidewalk is visible, so pedestrians appear to share the same paved lane with cars and parked vehicles.
Obstacles along the left frontage, including tables, planters, and stored items, can interrupt pedestrian movement and reduce effective walking width.
The street is relatively narrow and appears low-speed, which helps walking somewhat in the absence of formal pedestrian infrastructure.
There are no visible crosswalks, pedestrian markings, wayfinding signs, or curb extensions to support a more legible walking environment.
bikeability: There is no marked or protected bike lane anywhere in the scene, leaving cyclists to mix directly with motor vehicles.
The parked van and narrow shared roadway reduce lateral operating space for cycling.
The flat pavement and apparently low-speed residential context provide some basic conditions for very cautious cycling.
No bicycle parking, bike symbols, lane markings, or intersection treatments are visible to support convenient and safe bicycle use.
